hook: Norman Jouppi earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Northwestern University in 1980 and a PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1984, where he was one of the principal architects of the MIPS microprocessor. He spent much of his early career at Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory researching computer memory systems, microprocessor architecture and graphics accelerators, work that carried through DEC's acquisition by Compaq and Compaq's later acquisition by Hewlett-Packard, where he was named an HP Senior Fellow in 2010. He joined Google in the early 2010s and became technical lead for the company's Tensor Processing Units from their inception, with the first generation deployed in Google datacenters starting in 2015. He was lead author of "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit," published at ISCA in 2017, which documented the chip's real-world performance and became one of the most cited papers in computer architecture. He now holds the title of Vice President and Engineering Fellow at Google, continuing to lead AI infrastructure and TPU development.

standing.record: The site's records trace a single long arc through computer architecture: a master's degree in electrical engineering from Northwestern in 1980, a PhD from Stanford in 1984 where he was one of the principal architects of the MIPS microprocessor, then years at Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory researching memory systems, microprocessor architecture and graphics accelerators. That work carried through DEC's acquisition by Compaq and Compaq's later acquisition by Hewlett-Packard, where he was named an HP Senior Fellow in 2010, before he joined Google in the early 2010s. standing.standing: Norman Jouppi stands as the technical lead for Google's Tensor Processing Units, a role the records say he has held since their inception, and he now carries the title of Vice President and Engineering Fellow at Google. The first generation of those chips was deployed in Google datacenters starting in 2015, and he was lead author of the 2017 ISCA paper "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit," which documented the chip's real-world performance and became one of the most cited papers in computer architecture. The records credit him with more than 125 US patents and more than 125 technical papers, along with fellowships at ACM, IEEE and AAAS and membership in the National Academy of Engineering. His influence as recorded here rests on that infrastructure work rather than on any commercial or corporate control the site describes. Google is the only company on this site where he is listed as an executive.
